q: What is blended finance, and can an Indian MSME benefit from it?
title: Blended finance for MSMEs explained
short: Blended finance is public or development money used to make a project cheaper or safer for private lenders, through concessional loans, first-loss cover or grants. An Indian MSME rarely deals with it directly; it benefits through a bank or SIDBI loan that carries a lower rate, longer tenor or easier collateral because of it.

p: The OECD defines blended finance as the strategic use of development finance to mobilise additional finance for sustainable development in developing countries. In plain terms, a development bank, donor or government puts in money on softer terms so that commercial money will come in alongside it.

ul: Concessional credit lines: a development bank lends to SIDBI or a commercial bank at a low rate for a long term, to be lent on for a defined purpose such as energy efficient equipment.
First-loss or risk-sharing cover: public money absorbs the first part of any losses, so the lender asks for less collateral or lends to smaller firms.
Technical assistance grants: pay for energy audits, project reports or lender training, so the loan is easier to appraise.
Interest subvention: a government pays part of the interest, as in some energy efficiency schemes.

sections.h: How it reaches an MSME in India
p: Through the lender. SIDBI has run energy efficiency lines funded by development partners such as JICA, KfW and the World Bank, and banks take part in risk-sharing facilities. The MSME applies for an ordinary loan; the blended part shows up as better terms, an eligible equipment list and reporting duties after disbursement.

ol: A project that fits the line's purpose, often listed equipment or a measured energy saving.
An energy audit or detailed project report showing the expected saving.
Clean financial records and the usual KYC.
A way to report results after the loan, such as energy and CO2 saved.

example.title: Illustration: how a blended line lowers the lender's cost
lines: Loan: Rs 1 crore for energy efficient equipment
Lender's own funds: Rs 60 lakh at 10%; concessional line: Rs 40 lakh at 6% (illustrative rates)
First-year interest at 8.4%: Rs 8.4 lakh, against Rs 10 lakh at 10%, a saving of Rs 1.6 lakh
example.note: Rates are illustrative. The rate you are offered is the lender's decision; ask what concessional lines it holds.

senseible: Senseible's green loan readiness check and finance application put your energy and emissions records, read from bills and invoices, into the form a lender appraising a green project asks for. Loan terms and scheme eligibility are decided by the lender.
